doc.title: Carmen Lundy interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, February 15, 2023

chapter: Songwriting and recording Fade to Black
title: 'Eye of the Storm' and the Modern Ancestors concept
summary: Hurricane Andrew and family, her homage to Coltrane, Miles, Nina Simone and Dizzy, and wanting jazz vocal audiences to evolve.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Politics, race and the state of the country

blocks.x: Junior or with Gifton Garrett — I mean Giveton Gelin — and let’s see what that sounds like just to have them both. Let’s not just mute all that work you’ve done. You’ve done all this work why should we just mute it?” So that’s so wonderful to work with an engineer who also is a musician. Do you understand? It’s not just about dials and things, this guy’s a musician too. So I’ve evolved over the course of all these decades as a writer, as a singer. And some of it is a little bit of a, I’m a little bit in a quandary because I don’t understand why the audience wants me to come to the stage and give them “Street of Dreams” when I’ve got up “Flowers and Candles.” Okay, on “Eye of the Storm” is the perfect example okay? “Eye of the Storm.” My family is from Miami. I’m from Miami. And they were getting ready to see another horrific hurricane come through. And my family just happened to be one of those places on the planet that was devastated when Andrew came in back in the 90s. Okay? My family was nearly wiped out. And all the things that occurred subsequent to that, you know health issues and all kinds of other things that occurred with my family down there in Miami. So here it is like twenty years later or thirty, or whatever it is and there’s another storm pending and I’m in L.A. going oh. And I can hear that recall that they’re re-living, that nightmare. So “Eye of the Storm” was born out of that and also what was happening to the country politically. So there were two things going on at that time for the tune. So, but I knew that my concept of this record had to do with modern ancestors, okay, not the Sojourner Truths but the John Coltranes and the Miles Davises and the Nina Simones, okay, and the Carmen McRaes and so forth and so on. And everybody else knew that. And I’m from Miami and I have a huge love and appreciation for every contribution that Dizzy Gillespie and Chano Pozo created for Latin jazz you know, okay? So all these things I want. I’m sort of paying homage to — because these were my lessons, this is of my time. These are the ancestors, these are the ones that gave me the inspiration to do this. So that’s what “Modern Ancestors” is all about, is really kind of saying well I’m not one of them but because of them I’m me. You see? That’s a big thing. And I’m not sure if the jazz audience has really evolved along with me that way because the jazz vocal genre in and of itself has so much to do with music of a time that has to do with 30s, 40s, 50s, maybe some of the early 60s, maybe some of Bacharach stuff that happened in the 60s perhaps. So no one really is thinking what about jazz in 2022? Jazz vocal in 2022? Oh I see, that’s going to be [scats] okay fine. You want me to do that? Okay. But what about this? What about the little kid that’s hearing jazz for the first time that’s going to say, “I remember when I heard that lady, when my mommy took me to that concert.” “How old are you?” “I’m four.” It’s like what are they going to remember? I don’t want them to remember “Summertime.” I want them to remember “Flowers and Candles.”
